summary: Describes how delta encoding, sending only the differences between versions of a resource, can be added to HTTP/1.1 as a compatible extension. It can save bandwidth when a page changes a little. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: If you already have last week's newspaper, you only need to hear what changed. This lets web servers send just the changes.

questions: what is http status 226 im used
subtitle: How a web server can send just the changes to a page the client already has cached, as an extension to HTTP/1.1.

tldr.problem: When a cached web resource changes, HTTP/1.1 sends either nothing (304 Not Modified) or the whole new copy, even if only a small part differs.
tldr.mechanism: The client names its cached copy with If-None-Match and lists the delta formats it understands in a new A-IM header. The server may reply with status 226 (IM Used), an IM header and a body that is only the difference.
tldr.outcome: Responses can shrink and finish sooner, with only a few extra header bytes. The scheme is optional for clients, proxies and servers, and old caches are protected by the new 226 status code.

today: RFC 3229 is a Standards Track document published in January 2002, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends HTTP/1.1 as specified in RFC 2616.

sections.title: Why Send Only the Difference
sections.content:
HTTP caches let clients reuse earlier responses, and conditional requests check whether a cached copy is still current. But HTTP/1.1 keeps an all-or-none model: either the resource has not changed at all (a 304 response with no body), or the server must send the entire current value.

The authors point out that when a resource does change, the new instance is often substantially similar to the old one. The difference between them is a delta. A client holding the old copy could apply the delta to build the new one, which can cut response size and delay.

The goals are to reduce the mean size of responses, avoid extra round trips, keep per-request overhead low, support a variety of delta formats, interoperate with HTTP/1.0 and HTTP/1.1, stay fully optional, and allow moderately simple implementations. Delta encoding of request messages, or of responses to methods other than GET, is explicitly out of scope.
sections.eli5: Why mail a whole new book when only a few pages changed? Sending just the changed pages saves time and paper.

sections.title: Instances and Instance Manipulation
sections.content:
HTTP/1.1 terms like entity did not fit the idea well, so the RFC defines an instance: the entity a status-200 response to a GET would return right now for the selected variant of a resource, with zero or more content-codings applied but no instance manipulations or transfer-codings. An entity tag belongs to an instance.

An instance manipulation is an operation that can turn an instance into a partial or multi-message result. Range selection and delta encoding are the examples. The RFC places them in a fixed message-generation sequence: choose the variant, apply any content-coding, assign the entity tag, apply any instance manipulation, then apply any transfer-coding.

Because several manipulations may apply, order matters. A client who wants to finish an interrupted delta download needs the range applied after the delta. A client who wants part of the new content needs the range applied first. The RFC solves this with a range token in the A-IM header: the server MUST apply manipulations in the order the client lists them, and the IM response header lists the order actually used.
sections.eli5: Think of preparing a package in steps: pick the item, wrap it, label it, then maybe cut out a piece. The order of the steps matters, so the client gets to say what order it wants.

sections.title: How a Delta Exchange Works
sections.content:
The client sends a conditional GET with an If-None-Match header naming the entity tag of its cached copy, which identifies the old instance. It adds an A-IM header listing the delta formats it accepts, for example A-IM: vcdiff, diffe, gzip. If the entity tag is unchanged, the server returns 304 as usual.

If the resource has changed and the server can compute a delta, it replies with status 226 IM Used, an IM header naming the delta format used (for example IM: vcdiff), the ETag of the current instance, and a body holding the delta. The ETag describes the current instance, not the delta.

A server may always decline. A delta could be bigger than the resource, the server may lack CPU time, the resource type may not suit it, or none of the client's formats may be supported. A server that does not understand A-IM ignores it and sends a normal 200 response. If several formats are acceptable, the client can express preferences with qvalues, and the server picks.

A server MAY send a delta only if it could send a 200 response, the request has an A-IM header listing at least one delta-coding, and the request has an If-None-Match header listing at least one valid entity tag for the Request-URI. A delta response MUST carry status 226 and MUST include an IM header.
sections.eli5: The client says, 'I have version A, tell me what changed, and I understand these ways of describing changes.' The server answers with a short list of changes, or says nothing changed.

sections.title: Protecting Old Caches
sections.content:
The main risk is an older proxy cache that does not know about deltas. It might store a delta response and later hand it to an ordinary client, which would think it had received the whole resource. The RFC notes that the Internet still includes a significant number of HTTP/1.0 caches.

The fix is a new status code, 226 (IM Used), used for all instance-manipulated responses. The authors were reluctant to add a status code but saw no other efficient way to stay compatible with deployed HTTP/1.0 caches. They observe that existing proxies apparently forward responses with unknown status codes and do not try to cache them.

Some HTTP/1.1 rules could still allow caching a 226 response that carries explicit freshness headers. For that case the RFC defines an im Cache-Control directive. A cache that complies with this specification SHOULD ignore a no-store directive when im is present; all other implementations MUST ignore im and obey no-store.

The RFC warns origin server implementors that sending Vary: If-None-Match, A-IM on 226 responses is not enough to stop a proxy that lacks delta support from wrongly validating a cached 226 response.
sections.eli5: Old mailboxes might mistake a list of changes for the whole letter. So changed-only replies get their own special stamp, 226, that old mailboxes will not keep.

sections.title: Delta Formats and Base Instances
sections.content:
The RFC does not mandate one algorithm. It describes several, and registers three delta-coding values, vcdiff, diffe and gdiff, alongside the other instance-manipulation values gzip, deflate, range and identity.

  • diffe is the output of the UNIX diff -e command. It is fast and widely available, but deltas are relatively large and it works only on text.
  • vcdiff inherently compresses its output, generally gives smaller results than diff plus gzip, runs much faster, and can handle binary input.
  • gdiff is a generic, algorithm-independent format that is easy to implement but may not be the most compact.

A delta needs a base instance, an old copy the server still has. A server may keep none, only the latest prior one, all of them, or a subset such as the most recently used. To help, a client may send several tags in If-None-Match, and the server then MUST name the one it used in a Delta-Base response header. The server can also send a Cache-Control: retain hint, optionally with a number of seconds, suggesting the client keep that instance. retain=0 tells the client not to ask for deltas against it.
sections.eli5: There are different ways to write a list of changes, some short and some simple. The server also has to remember which old version you have, so it can mark which old copies are worth keeping.

sections.title: Headers, Caching and Content-Codings
sections.content:
Three headers carry the feature. A-IM is a request header listing acceptable instance-manipulations, each optionally with a qvalue; if it includes a delta-coding, the request MUST contain an If-None-Match header. IM is a response header listing the manipulations applied, in order; any response with an IM header MUST use status 226. Delta-Base gives the entity tag of the base instance. If the server cannot send anything acceptable according to A-IM, it SHOULD return 406 (Not Acceptable).

A client or proxy that receives a 226 response MAY decode it and store a normal 200 entry, decode all but range selection and store a 206 entry, or store the 226 response itself. A cached 226 entry MUST NOT be reused when the IM values do not appear (in the same order) in the new request's A-IM header, when the cache does not understand them, or when the Delta-Base or If-None-Match conditions do not match.

With content-codings, the server's Content-Encoding list SHOULD be a prefix of what it would have used without a delta, so the client can apply the delta without decoding. A proxy forwarding the reconstructed result MUST carry the same Content-Encoding as the delta response.

Compression with diffe or gdiff greatly reduces size, so implementations that support them are strongly recommended to support gzip or deflate as well. vcdiff is already compressed and does not benefit.
sections.eli5: The request says what kinds of change-lists the client can read. The reply says which kind was used and which old version it applies to. Caches follow strict rules so nobody gets the wrong page.

sections.title: Cost, Intermediaries and Security
sections.content:
The RFC estimates the overhead. Adding A-IM:vcdiff to a request is about 13 extra bytes. Against mean request sizes of 281 and 306 bytes from a study it cites, that is between 4% and 5% of a request, but only conditional requests carry it, so the mean increase would be much less than 5%, and probably below 1%. A delta response adds about 11 bytes for IM:vcdiff. The sender can skip the delta if it would not save space, so a delta-encoded response should never be larger than a regular response for the same request.

Proxies that understand deltas could do more. They might store delta responses, apply them to their own cached copies, generate deltas locally from a fresh cached copy, or convert a non-delta client's request into a delta request. These add complexity and may need more storage or CPU.

For data integrity, existing digests do not cover content assembled from several messages, and a mechanism is proposed in a separate document. On security, the authors say they are not aware of any aspect of the basic delta mechanism that affects the existing security considerations of HTTP/1.1.
sections.eli5: The extra label on each request is tiny compared with what a good change-list saves. Smart middlemen can help too, but they must work harder.
